Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 16, to authorize the governor in council to enter into agreements with the governments of the provinces of Canada respecting the vacation by the provinces of the personal income and corporation tax fields for the duration of the war.
He said: This bill received its first reading on March 23. There was very little discussion at that time because the house was requested to defer discussion until the bill was in committee on its second reading. At various times, however, the house has had an opportunity of discussing the general principles of the bill.
During the budget debate last year there was some discussion of the general principle. Then again there was discussion when vote 476 of the supplementary estimates for the last fiscal year was passed by the house. During the present session of parliament, various questions have been asked and statements made in regard to the dominion-provincial tax agreements, and the agreements themselves together with the correspondence with the provinces in regard to the agreements have been tabled.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: The completed agreements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
Not the
draft agreements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
No. I think the complete
agreements have been tabled; in fact I am sure that they have.
Vote 476 in itself constituted authority to enter into these agreements and to make the payments required thereby, excepting any payments arising out of the guarantee of provincial receipts from gasoline taxes. It had been the intention of the government to submit an estimate in each succeeding year for the term of the agreement covering the exact payments to be made to each province including any payments on account of the

Income and Corporation Tax
gasoline tax revenues. It will be remembered, however, that one of the provinces raised the question that while in signing the agreement it would be binding itself for the full term of the agreement, the compensating payments to be made by the dominion would be dependent upon the passing of an annual vote in the dominion parliament. I therefore agreed to introduce the present bill which would give continuing statutory authority to make the annual payments required for the duration of the agreements.
With regard to the general principles, as I have intimated, there has already been a great deal of discussion of the general principles of this bill, and I think the house is wholly familiar with them. This should make it unnecessary for me to make an extended statement at this time. Perhaps, however, I may summarize the essential features of the legislation and of the agreements.
What the provinces are required to do is to vacate the personal income and corporation tax fields for the duration of the agreement, which will run until one year after the cessation of hostilities, although, as the house will remember, provision is made by which any province may terminate the agreement at the end of any fiscal year if notice of its intention to do so is given in writing to the Minister of Finance, thirty days before such date. Income and corporation taxes are carefully defined in the agreements. In general, corporation tax includes any tax or fee the imposing of which singles out for taxation or for discriminatory rates or burdens of tax, either formally or in effect, corporations or any class or classes of corporations or any individual corporation, but excludes certain bona fide and reasonable licences or fees and business or occupancy taxes, and certain other taxes imposed by municipalities. Income tax is defined to mean any tax imposed upon the net income of a corporation or upon the net income or gross income of an individual or partnership, and includes a poll or head tax based on income. In compensation for the vacation by the provinces of these tax fields, the dominion agrees to make certain annual payments and to give as well a guarantee of gasoline tax receipts.
In regard to the annual payments, the house will remember that the provinces were given two options. They might elect either to receive an annual payment equal to the actual cash revenues received by the province from the taxes temporarily suspended during the fiscal year of the province ended nearest to December 31, 1940; or alternatively to receive an annual payment equal to the cost of the net debt service actually paid by the province during its fiscal year ended nearest
to December 31, 1940, not including contributions to sinking funds, less the revenue obtained from succession duties, during the said fiscal year. In addition, the offer I made in the budget provided that such annual payments might be augmented by providing fiscal need subsidies in cases in which it could be shown that these were necessary. This provision is implemented in the agreements which have been tabled in the house. The house will remember that the special amounts paid in recent years to the three maritime provinces and to Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia and which were voted annually by parliament were discontinued.
Finally, the agreement provides for a guarantee by the dominion of the amount of the net receipts by the province from gasoline taxes during its fiscal year ended nearest to December 31, 1940. I may add that agreements have already been entered into under authority of vote 476 of last year's supplementary estimates with all of the provinces except Quebec. In the case of Quebec, the provincial bill suspending income and corporation taxes and giving authority to the provincial government to enter into the agreement is either still before the legislature or has only recently been passed. It is my intention to sign the agreement with Quebec under the authority of the present bill, when it has been enacted, and when the necessary action has been taken by the province of Quebec, if it has not already been taken.
The bill itself is a simple instrument giving formal authority to the Minister of Finance, with approval of the governor in council, to enter into an agreement along the lines I have mentioned, with the government of any of the provinces of Canada and to make the payments and give the guarantees required. Two or three of the amounts contained in the agreement are incorrect in certain particulars. One of the amounts is incorrect because of a clerical error, and two of the others will have to be corrected to a very small extent by reason of small mistakes having been discovered since the bill was printed. Section 2 gives formal authority to enter into the agreements. It may be said that this section is unnecessary because of vote 476 passed last year, but I think it is desirable to have this formal authority set out in the terms of the statute. The statute is to be known as the Dominion-Provincial Taxation Agreement Act, 1942.
Section 3 provides continuing statutory authority to make annual payments to the provinces equal to the yield of the taxes temporarily suspended by the province, or
Income and Corporation Tax

to the cost to the province of its net debt service in the fiscal year ended nearest to December 31, 1940, with the deduction that I have mentioned. In the case of five provinces, namely, British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec, the option selected is the tax option, and the amounts payable are as shown in the bill, except that in the case of Manitoba the correct amount is $5,054,740.92 instead of $5,634,740.92. That is the clerical error which I mentioned. I should point out that the figures shown, like all other figures in the bill, represent the results of a careful audit of provincial books by an auditor appointed by the dominion for this purpose. The other four provinces, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Saskatchewan, selected the debt option, and the amount paid to each of these provinces is as shown in the bill. I would, however, ask the house to note the proviso clause at the end of section 3. It will be noted that any arrears of personal income and corporation taxes collected by the province after the close of its fiscal year ended nearest to December 31, 1940, may, in accordance with and subject to the terms and conditions set out in the agreement, be deducted from the annual amount payable to the province. The amounts so deducted are to be paid to the provinces after the termination of the agreement.
The general effect of this proviso is to assure that each province will have revenues accruing to it during the year following the termination of the agreement, and that the revenues during the war years will not be abnormally inflated. It is obvious that after the agreement terminates it may take some little time to get started again the collection of personal income and corporation tax revenues, and were it not for this provision provincial revenues would therefore be unduly low in the first year following the agreement.
Clauses 11 to 15 of the agreement deal with the way in which annual payments are to be made by the dominion, and the terms and conditions under which the deductions are to be made. Reference to these clauses will facilitate an understanding of the precise meaning of the proviso clause in section 3 of the bill.
Section 4 of the bill provides for the payment of fiscal need subsidies during each year of the term of the agreement to the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. When this clause is under detailed consideration by the committee I shall explain the basis upon which these fiscal need subsidies have been . 
calculated. I may point out however that in considering them the house should remember that the special grants previously voted annually to all the five provinces involved, as well as British Columbia, have been dropped. The amount of subsidy in the case of Nova Scotia should be $325,769.31 instead of the amount printed in the bill, $324,122.10.
Section 5 of the bill is the clause relating to the guarantee of gasoline revenue. The amounts set out after the names of the provinces represent the net receipts from the tax imposed by each province on the sale of gasoline during its fiscal year ended nearest to December 31, 1940, as determined by the dominion audit, except that the amount for New Brunswick should be $2,101,072.01 instead of the amount of $2,104,685.81 as shown in the bill. It is apparent that this section of the bill is going to prove a very important one for all provinces. In view of the increasingly severe war-time restrictions being placed on the use of gasoline and the shortage of rubber for rubber tires I am convinced that were it not for this tax agreement, including this particular clause, several at least of the provinces would inevitably have to face acute financial problems which presumably would have had to be solved otherwise by ad hoc solutions of a less fundamentally sound character.
Section 6 of the bill merely makes the payments to be made to the provinces pursuant to the agreements a charge upon the consolidated revenue fund and payable out of any unappropriated moneys forming part thereof.
Section 7 of the bill provides that the act shall be deemed to have come into force on March 15, 1942.
The bill by its nature is one which can be discussed more satisfactorily in committee of the whole house, and when we get into committee I shall try to answer any questions that may be asked by hon. members.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance has given us a rather meagre sketch of the provisions of this bill. As the subject is one which demands a great deal of study on the part of hon. members-and I trust they have studied these agreements-I desire to make some brief observations with regard to it, reserving detailed questions, as the minister has suggested, until we reach the committee stage.
It will be remembered that the genesis of this proposal was contained in the Rowell-Sirois report-in much larger form than the present arrangement; but that was its true origin. I assume every hon. member has read that report, especially the part relating to this

Income and Corporation Tax
matter. Hon. members will -recall that in consideration of the assumption by the dominion of the burden of unemployment relief and certain other social security measures, and of the deadweight cost of the provincial debt service, it was recommended in that report that the provinces should relinquish the tax on personal incomes and a multitude of other taxes levied principally against corporations, and succession duties. As hon. members know, the report itself proved abortive, or at least it was so treated that the proposals of the report were not adopted.
Now the minister has tried another scheme which as I apprehend it is not nearly so far-reaching as the recommendations of the Sirois report. But it is a very important matter. It strikes at one of the fundamental principles of our system of confederation. It constitutes a direct encroachment on the heretofore existing taxation rights of the provinces. I have no doubt that by certain of the provinces it has been agreed to with considerable reluctance. So far as my own province is concerned I would say that this agreement will be a benefit to it. The New Brunswick authorities have probably driven a rather good bargain with the minister; but there are some inequities and some inequalities with respect to the municipalities of that province, to which I have alluded on former occasions and to which I shall direct attention briefly this afternoon.
The question of the elimination of the provinces in the field of succession duties has been dropped. I regret that exceedingly. I am not an out-and-out proponent of the centralization theory, but it has its advantages. There should be one succession duty taxation measure in this dominion and one only. But that seems impossible of accomplishment. We have the spectacle in this country of the same dollar being taxed twice, if taxable at all; I could give examples of the same dollar of value being taxed at least three times. Of course that is only justified in the case of the dominion on the principle of necessity. I regret that the minister did not pursue his efforts to persuade the provinces to vacate the succession duty field. But I am aware of the extreme opposition that developed in certain provinces with respect to this important matter; they have looked upon that field of taxation as their own and are not willing to give it up.
These proposals in their present form certainly visualize the principle of encroachment upon provincial rights of taxation and upon the whole matter of provincial autonomy. I do not propose to raise any debate on that point. I know there are two schools of thought in this dominion, and that in some of the provinces provincial autonomy is
adhered to very strongly. But there is no doubt that the vacation by the provinces of the field of direct taxation in relation to incomes of corporations in favour of the dominion is a very distinct change and one more step towards centralization. I do not object to that at the moment, although if it were to be permanent it would deserve a great deal of study at the hands of the membership of this house.
Of course it may be argued that there are compensations. Undoubtedly there are. And I warn the house that the compensations that will be payable under this measure and under these agreements will be very much larger than any that the minister visualized when he made his former statement. It will be recalled that in his budget speech of April 29, 1941, the minister referred at considerable length to his offer to the provinces. In doing so he mentioned the position taken in a budget speech by his predecessor, the present Minister of National Defence. He stated then that after the most careful consideration of all the questions involved, the government had reached the conclusion that the rates of personal and corporation income taxes should be raised by the dominion to the maximum levels which would be reasonable at this time, if the provinces were not in those fields. Their plans were drawn therefore on that basis, and in due course, he said, he would outline proposals to increase the minimum rates of corporation income tax to 40 per cent; to increase the rates of personal income national defence tax. Then he put upon the record what the concrete proposals were, as follows-
-that the dominion will offer to pay each year for the duration of the war, to any province which, together with its municipalities, will temporarily vacate the personal income tax and corporation tax fields either
(a)	The revenues which the province and its municipalities actually obtained from these sources during the fiscal year ending nearest to December 31, 1940, or
(b)	The cost of the net debt service actually
paid by the province during the fiscal year ending nearest to December 31,	1940 (not
including contributions to sinking funds), less the revenue obtained from succession duties during that period.
Then he went on to say:
Such payments will be augmented by appropriate fiscal-need subsidies where it can be shown that these are necessary.
And he made the further declaration-
. . . it is proposed to discontinue the present special grants which are voted annually by parliament.
Income and Corporation Tax

Those are grants arising in the case of the maritime provinces out of the Duncan report and the White report, and special provisions made for the province of British Columbia.

And two others, namely,
Saskatchewan and Manitoba.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
Yes; for
the moment I had forgotten about them. Then the minister went on to emphasize that this was not an attempt to get the provincial tax field permanently. I have one observation to make in connection with this latter statement, and it is this, that having regard to the gigantic expenditures the dominion is obliged to make in respect to the war, I see no possibility of our vacating in any degree- at least, if at all, in a very minor degree- the high income tax rates we shall have to pay as the years roll by. We might as well face that situation. And if we are to have these high rates existing-and perhaps extended; who knows?-it would be the part of wisdom, taking the long range view, that some permanent arrangement should be made with the provinces to stay out of this field permanently. I offer that simply as a personal view, speaking on behalf of the taxpayers of this country, who, after all, have to bear the brunt of the whole thing. Of course I have no hope that anything I may say will have any influence in public policy with respect to the provinces. It is unthinkable that we should return to a system under which, on the same income, taxes would have to be paid three times. Such a condition would be unbearable; and it would not be the proper or the just thing to do.
Therefore I suggest to the minister that while he has emphasized -the point that this is only temporary, at least from the federal point of view, we should look forward to its being part of the permanent tax structure of the country. I suggest there should not be a return on the part of the provinces, or of the municipalities through the power delegated to them by the provinces under appropriate legislation, to the collection by them of income and corporation taxes.
I said a minute ago that I thought an examination of the figures would indicate that the minister's previous estimates were low. Without giving effect to the minor corrections which the minister has pointed out to-day-which in respect of Manitoba, by the way, is not so minor, being somewhere in the vicinity of half a million dollars-it will be observed that the total payments to the five provinces which have adopted proposal (a) aggregate $71,316,083.17, while the total payments under proposal (b) to the four provinces which have taken the option of 
servicing of the net debt, less succession duties, is $10,457,124.10, or a total of S81,773.207.27. Then there has to be added a further payment to five provinces, the maritime provinces and the two central prairie provinces of Saskatchewan and .Manitoba, the sum of $3,232,789.32, making a grand total payment of $85,005,996.59. Again there must be added, under a separate section of the bill, on the basis as stated, the amount calculated as equivalent to the net receipts of the province from the provincial gasoline tax during the fiscal year ending nearest December 31, 1940. In that connection the total gasoline tax guarantee is $56,738,519.76, and, as the minister had indicated, it may be much more than that. This makes a total possible commitment out of the dominion treasury of the huge sum of $141,744,516.45.
If hon. members will refer to the minister's budget speech of last spring they will find a table in which it is indicated that the minister estimated a net increase in dominion revenue, in a full year, as a result of the changes made-in the income and corporation tax fields, of $90,000,000. That is, the difference between $155,000,000, the yield from increases in existing taxes, and the payments by ways of grants of $65,000,000. or $90,000.000. I suggest to him that the excess of actual payments over the estimate made by him, and the possible expenditures on the gasoline guarantee, have made very considerable inroads into that estimated increase in revenue. Therefore the result will be somewhat disappointing. Of course the whole thing is a war measure, and we are assured at the moment at all events, that it is temporary, that it is only for the duration and that upon giving notice any province may withdraw.
The true test from the standpoint of the taxpayer, the citizen of this country, is the effect upon him. The objective of course is to raise revenues for war purposes. After all, the taxpayer is entitled to some consideration from the point of view of how it may affect him. It never was intended to give him any relief, judging from the increased rates imposed by the federal budget of 1941. From the point of view of the taxpayer there is really no relief; but there is one circumstance to consider. There is only one tax gatherer, only one taxing master, and that is something for which he should be devoutly thankful, even though the amount of money which he has to pay has not been lessened in any degree-indeed has been increased.
I have referred to the policy of centralization. I doubt if the fathers of confederation

[DOT]ever contemplated that we should go as far as we have gone even with this measure; but the fathers of confederation never contemplated that there would be a war of the calibre and character of the present war, or that the necessity for raising huge sums of money by way of taxation would be so pressing as it is to-day.
I have stated already that I believe the present situation should continue permanently rather than for the duration of the war only. Of course that is something which does not lie directly within the province of this parliament; there are nine legislatures which are parties to this agreement and which would -have to consent.

speechtext: The hon. member is an optimist. My own view is that the more money these people get the more they want and the more they want to spend, especially if it comes as easy as it does when it comes from the federal treasury.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: British Columbia is doing well.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
There is one quarrel-I will not dignify it by the use of the word "quarrel," but I would like to comment upon the fact that the figure is frozen at the 1940 level. This may raise some difficulty with the municipalities. I understand that in the negotiations with the provinces, -or with some of them at least, the minister was inflexible on that point. I should like to point out to him the injustice of that position as I see it. The 1940 income tax returns for the municipalities of New Brunswick were based [DOT]on 1939 incomes. The war began in September, 1939, and the increase in the national income as a result of war expenditures-I think we can all agree that the great increase in the national income has been largely the result of war expenditures-did not begin to filter down to the individuals who pay income tax until late in 1940 or perhaps in 1941. In my province, where we have no war industry, or no war industry of any calculable amount, very little of the increased national income has filtered down to the taxpayers of the province. I am giving New Brunswick as an illustration, but I believe the principle is much more applicable to provinces which have been receiving a greater portion of the national income than New Brunswick. In that province we are being frozen under this agreement at the 1940 figure, and that is less than justice to the province. The provinces and municipalities had every right to assume that with the increased national income, more would filter into provincial and municipal exchequers as the war proceeded and as the tempo of expenditure increased. That will not be true under this agreement. That position is not reflected in this agreement, and it ought to be.
Some of the municipalities in my province were just beginning to utilize the powers which had been delegated to them by the province with respect to taxation on incomes. Other more settled municipalities, such as the cities, had used these powers for many years.
I have paid income tax ever since I had an income. True the rate was not high, but we have always had to pay income tax. The effect of freezing the figure at the 1940 assessment based on the 1939 income, the prewar income, has been that there is a deficit in the budget of all these municipalities, and presumably of the provinces. It is true that the government is to reimburse the provinces the amount of the frozen figure, but that is not sufficient to take care of the difference between the 1939 income and the 1941 income, or the increase in 1941, or the still greater increase in the 1942 income. "Unless the municipalities are prepared to reduce their services, or to cut their expenditures-my experience in municipal affairs is that the municipalities are very well run, that there is little waste and that expenditures cannot very easily be cut-these deficits cannot be met.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: Is the amount not made up by the province?

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
The amount is paid by the federal authority to the province, which in turn reimburses the municipality, but this is based on the 1939 income which is assessed in 1940. In the case of my own city the tax is payable about the middle of the year. If I have made my position clear, it will be apparent that there is a gap there. The result has been that the municipal councils in figuring up their budgets for this year and succeeding years have had to fill this gap. They have gone to the legislature and the legislature has granted them authority to make new imposts. In my province these new imposts have taken two forms. First, there is a householder's tax which in effect is simply an increased tax on real estate. There is no doubt that this tax will bring in money, but I shall not go into the details as to how much it will be. This tax is being imposed by the cities of Saint John and Moncton. It is being placed on visible, tangible property which cannot escape. There is a legal lien against it. I say to the minister that we will have this tax upon our backs as long as we live, or at least as long as the present situation continues. I am not sure that I made my suggestion quite clear. It was that there should have been some flexibility with
Income and Corporation Tax

respect to these income tax receipts. In the case of the municipalities, they should be assessed every year. They could be audited eveiy year and then there could be either an increase or a decrease in the amount paid to the municipality, so that they would not have to resort to new imposts and new forms of taxation such as the one I have described.
The other impost is such that every stenographer now must pay a poll tax. Some people may say that that is all right, but the fact is that in my city everybody over twenty-one years of age, other than a housewife or a domestic servant, must pay a poll tax. These people are here to-day and' gone to-morrow; you may get it and you may not. If there is a deficit, what happens? You just heap a little more on real estate. I do not think any hon. member believes we should impose further taxation on real estate. The reasons are obvious. Real estate has always borne the brunt of municipal taxation. During the depression this load increased to such an extent that real estate became a liability instead of an asset. To-day real estate is just beginning to recover the position it held formerly as a good asset, but this new taxation makes its position that much more difficult. I suggest to the minister that if it is not too late the position should be revised.
I tell him frankly that this is my main objection to the bill.
I do not think it is equitable, I do not think it is fair, I do not think it is just, to freeze the amounts that are to be reimbursed to the municipalities, via the provinces, to the pre-war income position-because that is what it is. It does seem to me it would have been quite feasible in working out the mechanics of this thing to have the position reviewed every year so that we might have avoided a fixed impost, from which I feel we shall now never be free. That is the main objection I have to the general principle of this measure.
I want to refer for a moment to certain other features of the bill. The chief point I make against the agreements is the inflexibility of that one position, and I have no doubt that the municipalities have also made their representations. I do not know how far the minister dealt with the municipalities. I assume he saw them, but of course I can understand that he did not find it desirable or convenient to deal with them directly. I want to impress upon him again that it would have been much fairer to the municipalities, and of course much fairer to the provinces, particularly such a province as Ontario with a large income tax revenue, if there had been some flexibility, having regard

to the greatly increased national income which filters down through to all the citizens of our various provinces, so that as the war proceeds and expenditures grow greater they would receive a much larger share of the national income from year to year-unless of course the minister peremptorily takes the view that the increased national income should be taxable only by the federal authority. That may be the proper view to take; it is debatable. But the municipalities and the provinces have their social and other services to keep up and they cannot do it without money. The very fact that there are increased activities in a community make it incumbent upon a municipality to increase its own services and expenditures. Without going into details I can say that nearly all the cities of the maritime provinces have had to increase their police force, for example, and I know that the cost of fire protection has also been increased in some of the municipalities because of the increased tempo of war activity. But in the agreements no regard has been paid to these considerations.
I should like to call the attention of the minister to a few portions of the New Brunswick agreement, and then I shall be through. The New Brunswick agreement, as I have it, was tabled in the form of a draft. The minister says that the completed agreements were tabled in this house, but I am not aware that that is the fact. On April 22, over a month ago, on the motion of the hon. member for Hastings South (Mr. Stokes), an order of the house was passed for a copy of all final agreements entered into between the government of Canada and the government of any province with respect to this matter. This return, so far as I know, has not yet been brought down. I am subject to correction; if the return was tabled, it escaped me. I do suggest that while we should proceed with the second reading of this bill we should not take it up in committee until the minister has laid upon the table copies of the final agreements with the provinces, so that hon. members may study them. After all, hon. members from the different provinces are very much interested in this proposal.
It will take from the federal exchequer possibly $200,000,000 in a given year, and that is no matter of small importance. Aside from the war itself I do not know of any question which demands more study on the part of hon. members of this house than these agreements, and I hope they have given study to them. I will say frankly that I have not analysed completely all nine agreements; I have contented myself with a limited study of the agreement affecting par-

Income and Corporation Tax
ticularly my own province. I invite the minister, if he has not already done so, to lay on the table, at the earliest possible day, copies of the final agreements.
I am not opposing the principle of the bill, blit I do say that there are inequalities and injustices. I think on the whole the dominion has done well by the provinces in the amounts it has allocated to them. I sometimes wonder, after all_ the pleas that have been made for retrenchment so that every' dollar may be devoted to the war effort, why it is that some of our provincial governments-not all of them perhaps, but I think this remark will apply to most of them-show not the slightest evidence of retrenchment in what must be peacetime expenditures. Take the little province of New Brunswick with 500,000 people. This year they budgeted for the highest sum in the history of the province, away over $10,000,000. I think Nova Scotia perhaps is just as bad.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: Are they going to have an election?

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: No, I do not think there is an election coming. There are several reasons, I suppose. I should not attribute motives, but I hold this view: there is not the sense of responsibility among provincial governments that there ought to be, having regard to the difficulties of the taxpayers and the financial demands made upon them by this war. Because times are good, because there is a lot of money going through the country as a result of war expenditure, the provincial governments think they might as well have some of it. One of the most disgraceful things in the country to-day is the amount of money the provinces are making out of the liquor traffic. In the little province of New Brunswick in the year 1935 the net revenue from liquor was a little more than half a million dollars. Last year the net revenue of the province from government sales of liquor was away over two million dollars.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: The people must be buying more liquor.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
I sometimes wonder. I am not going to preach temperance here. My principles are pretty well fixed and they are not going to be changed at my time of life. But I read a statement the other day which astonished me. The total budget of the Christian churches of Ontario in a given year was something like ten million dollars, while the drink bill of Ontario was perhaps ten or twenty times that amount-I am not attempting to give the actual figures. Is that a creditable comparison? Governments are in this business
now for the profit there is in it. They ought to cut it down; the hours of sale ought to be limited. In New Brunswick they call it liquor control. It is not liquor control at all. It is liquor monopoly-that is what it is, and you and I, who perhaps do not spend any money in that way, witness the spectacle of somebody else paying what perhaps ought to be contributed to the provincial exchequer. I do not think it is creditable to the country. But that is by way of an aside. I had not intended really to say that at all.
My' experience over a long number of years indicates that the greater the amount of money that is given to a province, the more they will spend, and some of it in a very questionable manner. I am glad to think that the municipalities operate perhaps in a better manner. I have in mind the little city of Moncton, which last year cut down its budget by $80,000, a very creditable performance.
I do not intend to say anything more about this bill. I think it is in pursuance of a compromise policy which the government had in mind having regard to the failure of the Rowell-Sirois report, which the government, I believe, was prepared to sponsor if it got the consent of the provinces. I regret very much that there was failure on the question of succession duties, but that has gone now and it is hardly worth our while to speak of it here.
I suggest to the minister that in dealing with the provinces he was a bit too lenient with respect to the power to impose new imposts. There is a provision in the New Brunswick agreement which leaves the way open for the province to impose new imposts, not of this particular class or kind, but nevertheless permitting annual levies from which I fear the taxpayer will never escape.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Hanson) has spoken as he has, probably something more should be said before this bill passes. The leader of the opposition made three or four remarks with which I personally, and perhaps, a good many people whose views should be heard here could not agree.
First, may I say a word with respect to the need for the taking over by the dominion of the power to tax corporations and the power to tax personal incomes. The leader of the opposition expressed the idea, as I understood him, that never again in the history of Canada would it be possible for the dominion government to recede from this field, that from now on it would be obliged to retain the power to tax corporations and personal incomes; and

the reason he advanced, as I gathered it, was that there would be so heavy a burden on the dominion government after this war that in order to discharge the burden the government would require so much money that it would be impossible to raise it except by invading provincial fields of taxation.
Now, I readily concede that the leader of the opposition is completely on valid ground when he forecasts that the dominion government will have such a burden of financial responsibility that it will no longer be able to discharge that burden.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
I did not
say that or anything like it.

speechtext: Well, to what extent am I deviating from the principles which the leader of the opposition laid down?

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
What I
said was that the necessities of the occasion would compel the federal government to hold on to this type of revenue and, probably, to this amount of revenue. I never suggested that the Dominion of Canada would repudiate its obligations.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I certainly did not suggest that it would repudiate its obligations. I believe that if the leader of the opposition reads to-morrow in Hansard what I said he will find it very difficult to distinguish between the meaning of my words and the meaning of his.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
Then I
misunderstood the hon. member.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
True, the dominion
government will never be able to discharge the responsibilities which it is assuming as a result of the expenditure incident to this war, and the members of this house should be objective enough to face that fact squarely now and govern their behaviour for the future accordingly. I am not suggesting that the dominion government repudiate its debts, but I am raising this question: if the time comes that the dominion government has so many financial commitments that, no matter what means it uses, it will be unable to raise enough money by way of taxation to meet those commitments, will someone tell me what the dominion government will be able to do? Something simply must be done; if the dominion government is to be able to meet its commitments it must find a new source of revenue, which source of revenue must involve a great deal more than invading provincial taxation rights and rendering it next to impossible for the provinces to carry on their responsibilities under the British North America Act.

The leader of the opposition implied, I thought, a few moments ago that the provincial governments were more or less careless in the use of their money. I do not wish to misrepresent what he said, but the idea was that the more money you gave the provinces the more they would spend. Well, in a time like this, when people from end to end of this dominion are needing more social services every day, when they need more money for old age pensions, for state hospitalization, state medicine and a dozen and one other things long overdue in this country, and when you bear in mind the fact that the responsibility for these social services in large measure rests upon the shoulders of the provinces, what can we possibly expect but that the provinces will spend more and more money?
One matter which I hope to bring to the attention of hon. members is that of education. At the present time our provinces do not possess the financial resources with which to support adequately the educational responsibilities resting upon them. Teachers from end to end of this dominion are too poorly paid. Schools are too poorly equipped. We are neglecting our sacred responsibilities to the generations of the future by failing sufficiently to provide for the training of youth. That is only one thing for which the provinces need money.
My own impression from what I have seen is that the provinces are not spending any money carelessly. Theirs is the responsibility for building and maintaining roads. Consider my own province as an example. In Alberta there are 90,000 miles of roads, with not quite 800,000 people to support those roads. When you bear in mind the fact that the people of that province are spread all over it in little communities here and there, to such an extent that they need 90,000 miles of road; when you bear in mind the amount of telephone service, the amount of inspection service for schools, the amount of medical service, and scores of other things which are necessary tb provide adequately for the needs of that province, you can understand how the provincial revenues as they now are are tragically inadequate. Instead of the dominion government endeavouring at this time to invade the provincial taxation fields and take from the provinces some of that which they already possess, the Minister of Finance should be occupying himself with ways and means whereby he could increase their revenues by adding to them supplies of money from the dominion treasury. At once, those who have never looked forward in the matters of economics and finance will say, "Where is the money to come from?"

The money must come from somewhere, and if this generation of members of parliament lack the vision to see where it will come from, then I do not know what is likely to happen in this country. We may have too great a tragedy long before we are able to elect a number of members with vision. I hope the house will come to see that.
I thought it would be a good thing for members of this house who are interested in the subject if I were to read two or three excerpts from a book which I have here, and which I think every member of the house should read. It is called "Economic Tribulation," and the author is Vincent C. Vickers. It might be well for me to state who Vincent C. Vickers is, in case anyone should not have discovered that up to the present. Let me read from the introduction:
Vincent Cartwright Vickers was born on the 16th January 1879 and educated at Eton and Magdalen college, Oxford. He was a deputy lieutenant of the city of London, a director of Vickers Limited for 22 years, and a director of London Assurance, from which he resigned in January, 1939. In 1910 he was made a governor of the Bank of England, and resigned this appointment in 1919. Later he became president of the Economic Reform Club and Institute.
I should think a record like that would at least entitle this gentleman to respectful attention. His book was published in 1941; there is no doubt it is pretty well up to date. Let me read two or three quotations. I quote first from page 50:
If once we can decide w'hat it is that constitutes the barrier between the producer and the consumer, whilst both remain dissatisfied, we shall have discovered not only the main cause of the world's discontent and of the existing enmities and jealousies among the nations, but at the same time the true road to the peace of the world. If the producers are waiting to produce more, if ships are waiting to carry the goods, if there are railway and transport services wheresoever there is demand for them, then the fault must lie with the consumer. Why does he hold back the trade and commerce and progress of the world and prevent the consummation of a lasting peace by deliberately refusing to avail himself of the good things the world can offer him? The answer is obvious. The consumer cannot afford to buy more. He has not enough money. Let us discard all biased opinions and we shall find it possible only to arrive at one decision, that the health and welfare of the individual, the happiness of the community, the contentment of the nation and the peace of the world are mainly if not entirely a monetary problem.
And Mr. Vickers has not taxation nor borrowing in mind when he speaks of a monetary problem, as will be made abundantly clear by quotations which I shall read further on. At page 65 I read:
Strenuous efforts have been made over some twenty-five years to patch up the money system in an attempt to make it last a little longer, but it has stood and now stands in the way of progress and social betterment, thereby creating universal unrest and a tendency to obtain by force what cannot be obtained otherwise. For the sake of our children let us take warning in time. Let us discard the policy of inaction and pretence and boldly face the fact that it is not the inevitable smoke of the galley stove which assails our nostrils but that a fire is raging in the hold and that the ship of state is in imminent danger.
These words bear particularly on the discussion this afternoon:
Our democratic system and our existing financial system can no longer live together. One of them must give way to the other.
The measure we have before us this afternoon is a move in the direction of reducing the democratic rights of the Dominion of Canada.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: Or the provinces.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
Or the provinces; it is the same thing. You cannot think of Great Britain as a democracy without thinking of the democratic rights of the great cities and towns of England, the great counties of England. Wherein lie the true sources of democracy in England? In the towns and in the counties. And wherein lie the chief guarantees of democratic principles in Canada? In the towns and in the provinces. Destroy the autonomy of the provincial governments and you have struck an irreparable blow at democracy throughout the dominion.
I am going to read one more passage, which I think will show just the line along which Mr. Vickers' mind is running, and then I have a comment or two to make. When I have done that I shall have finished. At page 74 I read his suggestions for the future:
1.	State control and state issue of currency and credit through a central organization managed and controlled by the state.
2.	Stabilization of the wholesale price level of commodities. That is to say, a fixed and constant internal purchasing power of money; so that a pound will buy to-morrow what it bought yesterday; an honest pound, not a fluctuating pound. And this can be done by so issuing and regulating the volume of available credit and currency that it shall at all times be adequate to permit of the purchasing power of the consumer being equated with the volume of production; not by limiting the purchasing power but by firstly increasing purchasing power more in proportion to the productive capacity of industry.
May I pause a moment to make this comment. The measure before us is decreasing the purchasing power in the hands of the community.

speechtext:
Only a small portion of it. The more you examine it the more you will see the force of what I have said. While the provinces have struck a good bargain, the minister has made a good bargain too. Let me continue with the quotation:
Any additional supply of money should he issued as a clear asset to the state; so that money will be spent into existence and not lent into existence.
Again:
The fluctuating quantity of gold lying in the vaults of the banking system should never be permitted to govern the volume of credit and currency needed by the country.
Again:
The elimination of slumps and booms; and more direct procedure for eliminating unnecessary poverty.
And again:
The abolition of the debt system where all credit is created by the banks and hired out at interest to the country.
I should like to say just a word to the Minister of Finance. I realize how heavily burdened he is, how difficult is his task of guiding this country through this great crisis, and in large measure I sympathize with him. But let me tell the minister and tell this house that the minister can never successfully finance this war so long as he stays with the principles of the debt system of money. He will never create that happiness and union in this country which ought to exist so long as he thinks in terms of taking away from someone what he has, so long as he thinks of reaching out and invading provincial fields of taxation and filching from the provincial governments the means of obtaining the money which they need to discharge their responsibilities to their people. And he will never succeed so long as he thinks in terms of centralizing power at Ottawa. Sometimes in listening to hon. members such as the hon. leader of the opposition I wonder whether they have forgotten entirely that Ottawa was created by the provinces, that the first political organizations which we had in this country were provincial organizations, and that the provinces put Ottawa here to do work for them, not to dominate them, not to render their position impossible.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: Confederation was a mutual arrangement.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: Exactly, but the fathers of confederation never envisaged a time, we may be sure, when Ottawa would grow into a huge colossus threatening the very existence of the provinces.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: They never envisaged a time when we would grow into a nation either.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: I am afraid I do not grasp the significance of that remark. Did they imagine that the confederation when first formed was not a nation?

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: No, definitely no, we were not.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: I wonder what the hon. member has in mind. Does he look upon a nation as being an organization of people dominated completely by a central power, or does he look upon a nation as an organization of great units which can pull together?

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: Exactly; the latter is my conception of a nation, and that is what was brought about by confederation.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: Then how does the hon. member say that the fathers of confederation did not visualize a nation?

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: I say they never visualized a nation that would take the place in the world that Canada occupies to-day. We are now taking a place as one of the most important nations in the world, such a place as the fathers of confederation never visualized; consequently we must take on national proportions, and we cannot do it as long as we are divided provincially.

speechtext: There is no need for division provincially. There are eight provinces in this dominion that are as vitally concerned in the conduct of this war as the dominion government is.

speechtext: Then why all the argument? Let my hon. friend vent his spleen on those he needs to quell.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
There is a way of
managing this dominion without resort to these hurtful and offensive measures. There is no need of such an abomination as was proposed in the Sirois recommendations, to hamstring the provinces of this dominion. There is no reason why every province should not be majestic in the greatness of its autonomy. No province in this dominion desires anything which is not in the interest of the whole dominion, and surely Ottawa ought to be looking only to that which is in the interest of the whole dominion.
It is possible so to organize and manage the finances of this dominion that the provinces can be peaceful and prosperous and happy and strong. But measures such as the bill now before us are not the kind which will produce that desired result. If this dominion is to reach a position where it can discharge its responsibilities with respect to the debts accruing during this war, the dominion government must adopt the principles which Mr. Vincent Vickers laid down, particularly the one with respect to the state control and state issue of currency and credit; the one in which he says that any additional supply of money should be issued as a clear asset to the state, so that money will be spent into existence and not lent into existence; and the one expressed in the words "the abolition of the debt system where all credit is created by the banks and hired out at interest to the country."
In my judgment the minister should be coming to this house asking for authority to establish in Canada a currency commission through which he could issue the amount of money which the goods and services producing and consuming power of this country would support without causing inflation. If he were occupying the time of this house with that proposal he would be dealing with a measure by which a solution of the vexatious problems which confound the people of Canada could be found, and there would be no reason whatsoever for weakening in any respect the autonomy of the provinces or impairing their financial stability.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR VACATING TAX FIELDS AND ARRANGEMENTS FOR SUBSIDIES
speechtext: I am in agreement with the general principle of this bill. I believe that the principle of having one agent collecting these income taxes and corporation taxes is sound. Moreover I am in agreement with the sentiment ex-

pressed by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), that by taking over from the provinces two of their most flexible and expanding sources of income and replacing them by fixed amounts over a period of years we are handicapping the provinces in the field of social service.
The fathers of confederation, to whom reference has been made, very rightly I think gave to the provinces certain powers of taxation. Undoubtedly they never visualized such fields as income tax and corporation tax, certainly not in the immensity to which they have now grown. But they left with the provinces control of certain public services that they must have known would be found to cost the provinces increasing amounts from year to year. To compensate for those services which were certain to become more costly the fathers of confederation left the provinces with certain fields of taxation which also were possible of expansion.
I am thinking particularly of two services in the field of social services, namely, health and education. We take away from the provinces the right to collect income and corporation taxes, the two fields in which provincial income has been expanding in the past. We leave them with the responsibility of taking care of health and educational services, with the result that we are forcing them to sell liquor in order to provide our boys and girls with educations.

Does the hon. member
want them to stop it?
Stop what?
Stop selling liquor.

I certainly would
like to see the selling of liquor curtailed during the war.
Are you against the selling of liquor, or do you want to curtail it?

That is not the
point I am discussing. My point is that when you take away from the provinces their two greatest sources of revenue, sources from which they would probably derive continually increasing amounts, and saddle them with social services, the costs of which increase from year to year, you leave the provinces only two other expanding sources of revenue, those from the sale of liquor and gasoline. For the duration of the war the sale of gasoline will be regulated, so that there is no source of income open to the provinces which can increase in large amounts from year to year, except that derived from the sale of liquor.
Income and Corporation Tax

The leader of the opposition quite properly-pointed to the rigidity of the amount to be returned to the provinces, and suggested that a certain flexibility in the amount payable might have been better. I suggest it would have been in the interests of the nation if, when adopting a flexible amount, and taking over these sources or revenue, the dominion had at the same time undertaken at least a partial responsibility for some of the social services which are expanding, and which will continue to expand from year to year.
The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has called attention to the state of education. When our schools open in September four thousand class rooms will be manned by unqualified teachers. Fully 120,000 young people beginning in September will be placed in charge of teachers without any professional training. That circumstance is brought about largely by reason of the fact that the public school teacher can go into a war industry and earn double the amount he or she can earn teaching school. Our educational system is left to be largely the responsibility of local communities. Our provinces are most reluctant to assume more than 10,	12
or 15 per cent of the cost of that public service. The result is that we are getting the type of education that the local municipality is capable of providing.
If in this bill, instead of taking from the provinces this source of revenue and returning to them a frozen sum to replace the amount taken, the dominion government had assumed a certain percentage of the cost of those increasing provincial services, I believe it would have been a proper procedure. After all, these are national services. The type of education a boy or girl gets is surely a matter of national responsibility. The boy or the girl may not remain in the municipality or in the province in which he or she was born. When the boy in adolescence or manhood moves to some other province he becomes the responsibility of that province. He becomes a national responsibility, just as health is a national responsibility. We are finding that out to-day in our enlistment figures, when we take note of the number of young men who in the prime of life are rejected through physical unfitness.
We have long passed the day when the dominion government should have begun to realize that these two vital services are of national importance, and should have undertaken to accept some responsibility for them. That, it is true, is the responsibility of provincial governments, as set out by the British North America Act. But I suggest that in making this financial arrangement with the provinces, under which the sources of revenue
[Mr. Noseworthy.T
are taken over by the dominion, instead of giving a fixed amount of money in lieu thereof the dominion should accept a percentage of the responsibility in respect of those expanding, ever-increasing national services, namely health and education.
Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South): Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay, unnecessarily, the passage of the bill, but one or two things I believe should be said. So often we have heard protests from various provincial governments respecting the inroads the federal authority is making on provincial jurisdiction. It is quite true we are doing that. But after listening to the last two speakers one is almost led to the belief that they are advocating the taking over of all the services by the federal government. They say at least that we ought to pay more for this and ought to pay more for that.
We are now in a period of war. The minister of lands and forests in any province has practically nothing to say about the administration of his department, because the sale of timber, the cutting of timber and everything in that connection is under the jurisdiction of the timber controller, an officer of the dominion government. I am not one who says that we should do away with provincial governments; but if we are going to ask the federal government to take over the responsibilities indicated by the last two speakers, namely, the leader of the New Democracy group, and the hon. member for York South, then we might just as well come to the point where the federal government is going to take everything over. The last speaker referred to the possibility of taking over some of the social services.
The cost of them.

Well, if you take over the cost you take over the service; what else do you do? The fact of the matter is that if one looks over the various social services in Canada he will find that we have a checker-board system. I was astonished the other day by the replies I received from some hon. members from Saskatchewan when I asked them to give me figures showing the amounts paid under the mothers' allowance provisions in that province. I asked for the information because of comparisons which had been made in my constituency with respect to payments made in Ontario and in Saskatchewan. To my mind the payments in Saskatchewan were absolutely inadequate, but perhaps to the minds of those in Saskatchewan they were adequate.

What minds?

Income and Corporation Tax
Those who put it through, or who brought it into force.
They cut their garments to suit their cloth.

It is time we did that in a great many instances. If we have not the cloth we should try to get it. We get it for war purposes; let us get it for paternal legislation. When we begin to compare things we find that we have a checker-board system across the country. Some provinces have not the social legislation that other provinces have.
So far as this bill is concerned I consider it to be a war measure. It may end up eventually as a national measure that will always be in effect, that will always be the law of this country. The various provincial governments, having studied this matter, I hope carefully, have decided to enter into agreements with the Minister of Finance of Canada under which they make certain concessions. I feel that these things may have to be regulated as time goes on. Apparently this is leading eventually to a general federal policy under which the provinces will no longer collect either succession duties or income tax. I believe that all the provinces are asking for is that the responsibilities which are theirs under the British North America Act should be taken over by the federal government and be of no particular burden to the provinces.
While I am critical of some of the provisions of this bill and of some of the arrangements to be made under it, we must face the fact that we are at war. No matter how great a burden it may be upon the provinces, no matter how difficult it may be for them to meet their obligations, for the time being we are at war and we have to do everything we can to win that war. If we do not win the war there will be no succession duties and there certainly will be no incomes. Let us make up our minds to the fact that we will all be enslaved by an enemy who will not care whether we have food or incomes. While there are certain provisions of this bill with which we are not in accord, it is a war measure and so far as we know now will be only for the duration of the war. When the war is over we can debate this measure, we can debate matters of social legislation and paternal legislation and other things which are not only in the minds of members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. The members of the C.C.F. often pose in this house as being the only ones who look after the so-called working people, the farmers and others in this country. We are all Canadians, whether we are industrialists or otherwise, and our sympathies are with Canada. We want to act in the best interests of Canada and in the best 44561-1724
interests of the working people and other classes of people in Canada. That does not rest only with the C.C.F.
Actions speak louder than words.
Actions speak louder than words, and the people know what we have done.
You had plenty of time to correct the abuses.

You certainly have not corrected the abuses either. In spite of the argument that can be made against this legislation I feel that it is in the best interests of Canada and in the best interests of our war effort that it should be passed. When the time comes to have a readjustment of the equalities or inequalities under these acts, it will be after the war. The first essential of this and other legislation must be the winning of the war.

and the following enactments-

which sum-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot put any dollar value on it. The dominion is now free to increase its income tax to the level which the people of the country should properly be asked to bear. Releasing money for loans and savings certificates?

No; in taxes. While the provinces were imposing income taxes and corporation taxes, and the municipalities were doing the same, then, whenever a minister of finance approached his budget, he had to examine a variegated picture. He had to

The dominion now has the field clear to itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It gives a clear field to the dominion and enables the dominion to impose equitable taxation, the same weight on persons with the same capacity to bear that weight, whether they live in Vancouver or in Halifax or in any other part of the country. Perhaps I should say it became so important when taxes became so high. It would be important under normal conditions, but it is extremely important in a time of war.
It will equalize taxation throughout the country.
