national income is going to be very much greater than it otherwise would be, and the dcminion government are responsible. They have to get, by loans and taxation, money with which to meet that enormous expenditure. From my point of view at least, it is hardly fair to us to be paying out these billions of dollars and increasing the incomes for the benefit of the provincial income tax revenues. It means in the normal course that the provinces will have large and ever larger surpluses and we shall have large and ever larger deficits, and it is perfectly fair to freeze the amount that the provinces get from income tax and corporation tax sources at the level which existed at the beginning of the war. That is one theory that underlies these provincial agreements. It may be that this freezing, so to speak, will prove an advantage rather than a disadvantage to the provinces. It may be that personal incomes and corporation incomes, as a result of price ceiling policies, will not increase as the years go on, and it may be that the provinces are getting more out of this arrangement than they would otherwise, but I do not think so. I think that normally the income tax and corporation tax would rise; the arrangement is fair enough for the proy-inces, as long as they are assured of a pretty heavy return from income and corporation taxes; and the period taken was not unfavourable for the provinces. It is reasonable that they should take that amount and that the dominion should undertake to pay them that; and in view of the income created by enormous dominion government expenditures, which will bring tax returns up as the years go on, I think the taxation on that income should come back for the benefit of the dominion.
For war purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

It is based on the 1939 income, and that was for the most part a period of depression. I do not think it can be said that we were clear out of the depression before the war came. As a matter of fact, I am inclined to the other view, and one point I tried to make against this agreement was the freezing of the returns to the provinces, and to the municipalities in my province, at a figure based on a pre-war period, which might be said to be more or less a depression period. There is no doubt that in New Brunswick, there was in the municipalities an increase in the 1940 assessment over the 1939 assessment. That is why I think there should have been a little flexibility. I am impressed with the
{Mr. Ilslqy.]
argument of the minister that if they were allowed to go on, having regard to the rising rate of national income due to federal government expenditures, they would have had what I might call an unearned increment or something of that sort.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A windfall.

A windfall. I think there is something in that. I still think, however, that it should not have been frozen on the 1939 income. The minister, I understand, was pretty inflexible about that, and I should like to know the reason why. Is it because he felt that there was substantial government expenditure in 1940 which should not be taken into account.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I took the actual tax receipts in the year 1940.
Yes, but that was on 1939 income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, in some cases, and in some cases it was not. I would not condemn the 1939 income too readily. A great many companies had a fine year in 1939; a good many taxpayers had a good year; their inventories were enhanced in value at the end of the year for some reason.
There was a war on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The last four months of 1939 were war months, and income was not poor at all. However, it is a matter of judgment as to what year to take and how to select your year. We did the best we could in taking the fiscal year which ended nearest to December 31, 1940, and we stuck to it. The leader of the opposition says I was inflexible. I certainly was, because if there was one feature of this agreement that one had to stick to it was that. If we began varying the amount payable to the provinces according to an estimate-

It would not be an estimate; they could make their assessments. I understand how it could be worked out. I think the minister could have given more effect to that theory. However, he has not, and these agreements do not incorporate it, so I suppose it is a waste of time to discuss it now, except to point out the position.
Coming back to the point raised by the hon. member for New Westminster and my colleague, we have on one side 185,000,000 of which we are certain. I suppose there is no chance of these people from the provinces coming back and asking for more, on the basis of fiscal need. Later I am going to ask about these grants for fiscal need. It looks to me

Income and Corporation Tax
like a hand-out. I should like to know something about the basis. On the other hand we must know with some degree of certainty what we are getting to balance this $85,000,000, plus the contingency arising out of the gasoline guarantee. Certainly it will amount to a substantial sum if things go as they are going now. Last year the minister said it did not amount to much, $50,000, which is really nothing. But we had a 10 per cent increase in corporation income taxes plus excess profits tax. The department should know what that means because they have the returns in. The personal income tax returns were in by March 31 at the increased rates. The corporation income tax returns were in by April 30. I do not know if they have been compiled yet. While the amounts are not fixed, there must be some estimate of what the increased taxes arising out of the 1941 budget total, which are to compensate for and out of which the dominion government pays this $85,000,000 plus the guarantee. If we are not going to get $85,000,000 plus the guarantee we did not make a very good bargain. I think the minister should give that information, or he should ask that the committee rise until it is obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think that information could be obtained in such a form as to be of any value. The estimate that the leader of the opposition read was that $90,000,000 additional would arise from the increased income tax rates-
That has nothing to do with this.
But I am offsetting it against the $85,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; that has to do with it. The question I understand is, how much money shall we get from the increase in income tax and corporation tax rates which these agreements make possible. Is that not the question?

Not quite that. You could have had the increased rates without these agreements at all; but we all agree that it would have been inequitable to do so. However, you made the agreements; you got these provinces to vacate the field; you buy them off to the amount of $85,000,000. What are you going to get to recoup these outlays? The minister made an estimate of $90,000,000; that is how I interpret the figures of his last budget speech. If that is all, it is hardly worth while. I think myself it will be more. But when you take into account the contingent liabilities that the government has incurred with respect to the gasoline guarantee you may find a deficit on this instead of a credit.
Mr. 'ILSLEY: The liability under the gasoline tax guarantee should not be set off against what we get, because we would have been obliged to look after the provinces in some way. If by putting in gasoline regulations we take ten or twenty million dollars off the revenue of a province like Ontario we could not shut our eyes to that. It might not be so fatal in the case of Ontario, although their gasoline tax revenue was $26,000,000 in 1940. We would have been obliged to do something; we cannot bankrupt a province by our acts without some provision. What would have happened would have been that the provinces would come here and by pressure, by successful presentation-
They would have had a case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; by way of advocacy they would have argued for this and that; we should have been obliged to work out something as fair as possible; and I doubt if it would have been as fair as this.

The minister says that if he had not given the gasoline tax guarantee it would have been inequitable to pass the rationing regulations and such things. What has the minister to say about this question of price-fixing? He did not think much of it in 1941. In the debate on the address in November, 1941, he condemned the whole policy of price-fixing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think so.

I have not the minister's words here; I will send upstairs and get them. However, that is only in passing. What does he think of the situation brought about by the price-fixing policy? Is he going to bankrupt all the small grocers? By adopting a policy of rationing tires and gasoline he has put out of business an army of men who were engaged in selling automobiles. Does that appeal to the minister as ethically wrong? In the United States I read that they have appropriated $600,000,000 or so to take care of the wreckage of that business. We have not done anything like that in Canada. And, believe me, that business is a wreck. If you do not believe me, go to any of the big garages in this country that were engaged in selling automobiles. You will see men vainly striving to adjust themselves to the condition, coming to Ottawa to try to get some part of the "bits and pieces" programme, with very little success. I think there is a man in this city to-day; there was last week, from a big, well-equipped garage

Income and Corporation Tax

in New Brunswick, who was trying to get something to help save his investment. On the same principle as applies to the provinces and the gasoline tax, what does the minister say he should do for these people? Take the corner grocer who, before the price-fixing, sold peas based on a certain cost, not on replacement cost at all. To-day he has to sell at the same price, which may be three cents a tin less than they cost him. What is going to happen to him? Either he must sell these peas at a loss or not handle peas. The same thing will apply to his whole stock in trade. The result is that he has either to do business at a loss or to go out of business. They are going to the wall just as fast as they can. What is the government going to do for these men?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not admit that that is the situation at all.

I can
demonstrate it. The minister living here in Ottawa does not know what is going on round him, and his people do not tell him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman
say that bankruptcies have increased?

I have
not any figures, but I know that men tell me, "I just cannot go on if I cannot have a cent or two on my prices." These men are not profiteering, they just want a chance to live, and they are not being given a chance. However, this is aside from the point we have been discussing. But I think I ought to tell the minister that the retail trade in this country is suffering. It is suffering because of the inflexibility of the position taken by the government with respect to prices. There is going to be no subsidy for these men. Perhaps something ought to be done with respect to the cost of production, so that there could be a spread between them and the wholesale. But there is no doubt that these men either must sell certain commodities at a loss, or must not sell them at all. If you carry that far enough, they are out of business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, these are very general
statements, and they are irrelevant to the discussion.

I agree
with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member mentioned some commodity; was it tea?

I believe
it was peas.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it will be found that the hon. member's statements are entirely too broad, and that they are not justified by the

facts. Certainly an enormous amount of work has been done in giving reasonable protection to people in business in connection with the application of this price-ceiling policy. I might have said what I thought was happening in the instance to which the hon. member has referred, but I am not quite sure enough of my facts to make a statement.

If the minister wants an
illustration I will give him one to which my attention was drawn to-day. I refer to a merchant right in this city who is selling cured meats, and who has found himself in a position in the last three weeks of having orders he cannot fill. The price ceiling has limited the market to such an extent that he cannot get meat to cure. Then, he has had trouble with the Department of Munitions and Supply. He used his car to deliver from his wholesale producing plant to local grocers. It was a touring car, not a truck, and he received a C-3 permit. Yesterday that permit was called in, and he has received an A-l permit which will not permit him to deliver his goods. I have just drawn this point to the minister's attention, although perhaps the discussion is wholly irrelevant. However, my observation would lead me to believe that the small independent retail grocer or the small business man, by subsidies more than by fixing, is being submerged to a level where he cannot get the commodities at a price at which he can retail to the public, and at the same time compete with the mass production carried on in chain stores and cooperative enterprises. That is definitely the situation in this section of the country, and particularly in the city of Ottawa where the independent retailer in the merchandising business is paying a very, very severe penalty for price fixing.
I am not going to refer to the question of price fixing, but I wish for a moment or two to speak respecting the small business man, whose position was mentioned by the leader of the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not wish to be too strict, because I always hope that these little flurries will die down, but when the debate reaches a point where it is one of another subject entirely, I feel I have to raise a point of order.
Mr. O'BRIEN: Perhaps the point I wish to make might be brought up more properly on section 5. However, there is a broad principle which might be discussed under this section. I understand the tax on gasoline sales has been fixed as of the year 1940. In view of the rationing of gasoline, which has been so severely inaugurated in the maritime

Income and Corporation Tax
provinces, there would seem to be a great danger of loss in revenue, due to the fact that cars will not be put on the road. New Brunswick-and I speak particularly for it, believing that the other maritime provinces are in a somewhat similar position-will lose a great amount of revenue which it formerly received from that source. I am just wondering if at the time these agreements were signed there was any provision whereby because of some act of the federal government, such as the procedure of rationing, a further study could be made to compensate provinces for changes which were unforeseen when the agreement was signed.
Then again, in somewhat the same category might be placed the sales of liquor. If it was expected that those sales would 'bring in a certain revenue, as was the case with respect to motor cars when the agreements were signed, in the event of some change being made by the federal government can the provinces ask the minister for a reconsideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The fiscal needs subsidies
were fixed once and for all, and were not based on the principle of flexibility. That principle had to be decided at an early stage in the discussion with the provinces.
They were merely hand-outs, were they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; fiscal needs subsidies are, in my judgment, necessary to enable the provinces to carry on. I could give reasons why they are.
We shall come to that later.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It must be remembered that part of the time critics are saying that we have not made adequate provision for the growing requirements of the provinces and the municipalities, and the other part of the time they are criticizing what we are giving as a mere hand-out.

That
feature is certainly a hand-out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But, with regard to the
point raised by the hon. member for Northumberland, New Brunswick-
Which, by the way, was the same point I was going to raise, but the minister objected to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then the hon. member for Davenport made a bad introduction, if he was going to speak on that point.

Maybe I did; but I did
not get a chance to start.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thought the hon. member for Davenport was beginning a sympathetic examination of the problems of the small business man. That was the subject upon which he was launching.
The point raised by the hon. member for Northumberland, New Brunswick, namely that of revenue from motor car licence fees, was given careful consideration. It is an important element in the revenue of New Brunswick. It is also an important element in that of Nova Scotia, and also in that of some of the other provinces.

We have there, I believe, the highest tax in the world.
Mr. O'BRIEN: On automobiles.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whethei they are record taxes or not, but I know they are important.
They are.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My information is that for this year, 1942, there will be no important diminution in revenues from car licence fees. However, it is feared there will be an important diminution in 1943.
Mr. O'BRIEN: May I interrupt to say that licences in New Brunswick are sold in two divisions; that is they are sold for half years. That might be an important factor there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It might be a factor, yes. But answering specifically the question the hon. member asked, I must say that no provision is made for that affecting the fiscal needs subsidy. When the request was made that a guarantee be given with respect to the revenues from car licence fees, similar to that with respect to revenues from gasoline, I declined to give it favourable consideration. I said that if we were to examine all sources of revenue, the dominion perhaps should be receiving a guarantee that a certain amount of the service should be taken over by it. For example, if liquor revenues and car licence revenues were considered together instead of separately, and were frozen at the level of 1940 or 1941, probably the province would sustain a substantial loss.
And the minister might have added marriage licences, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
While some of the provinces would have liked an arrangement whereby they could have obtained a guarantee of all the revenue that we are likely to take, and had been left free to keep the surplus of all
Income and Corporation Tax

revenues we are likely to raise, I did not consider that would be a fair arrangement for the dominion-and neither it would have been. If something very bad happens, I suppose the matter can be considered, but in connection with these agreements the fiscal needs subsidies are not to vary.
Mr. O'BRIEN: If it is the result of action by the dominion government, then the dominion government should consider the situation more favourably than it has.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I never can say what will be done in any particular emergency, but the government will have to discharge its responsibilities when the time comes. I do not want to lay down the general proposal here that we are going to guarantee absolutely that the provinces will be kept in a particular position. The gasoline matter is so big and so important and fundamental to the revenues of the provinces that I say that we could not do something drastic like prohibiting altogether the use of gasoline for pleasure driving, a prohibition which might possibly come during the war, and shut our eyes to the financial consequences to the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the leader of the opposition this afternoon asked me to try to get some figures indicating the increase in the revenue derived from income tax for 1941-42 over 1940-41. The hon. member for Yale put the problem in this way. He said: The man on the street may say to me, "In order to get the provinces out of the income and corporation tax fields, you as a member of parliament voted and paid out to the provinces $84,500,000 to $85,000,000. To what extent did the dominion recoup itself?" I expressed the opinion that it would be impossible to give an answer to that in figures. I tried to outline some of the advantages from the point of view of taxation policy which accrued from getting the provinces and the municipalities out of the field, but I did not think a value in figures of any accuracy could be put upon that advantage. I have, however, ascertained the increase in revenue from national defence tax, personal and corporation income tax and excess profits tax for the twelve months ending May 31, 1942, there being a small element of estimate in that figure,
lMr. Ilsley.]
compared with the revenue for the twelve months ending May 31, 1941. The increase is startling, tremendous; it is $347,200,000.

That
would be partly attributable to the increased rate. The minister lumps the three together. Can he give the figures for income tax alone, divorced from excess profits tax and national defence tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The increase in personal and corporation income tax alone is $105,100,000.
Therefore the minister's estimate of $90,000,000 was really under the actual figure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The two are not comparable. One must put them all in because the increase in the tax on corporations from 30 to 40 per cent was an increase in excess profits tax. The corporation income tax is 18 per cent, and we did not change it. We increased the minimum excess profits tax from 12 to 22 per cent, and therefore the excess profits tax must be included with personal and corporation income tax in any fair comparison. National defence tax should be in there too, because that is really an income tax and was part of our total increase in taxation provided for in the 1941 budget. It is not fair to say that we have paid out $84,500,000 and that we have got in return $347,200,000.
Not to put it bluntly like that, I agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, for two reasons. In the first place we could have increased our income and corporation tax and the national defence tax to some extent, even if the provinces and municipalities had stayed in the field. As a matter of fact, we increased the excess profits tax and the income tax on corporations from 30 to 40 per cent, an increase of 10 per cent of the income, but we calculated that the provinces were collecting only 7 per cent, so in that case alone of corporation and income taxation we put on a little more than we got the provinces to take off.
That is my understanding.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is the first qualification of this figure which must be taken into account. The second qualification of course is that this tremendous increase of $347,200,000 for this year over last year is not due entirely to an increase in the rate but partly due to an increase in business.

Income and Corporation Tax
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No hon. member need be under the apprehension that we are paying out this $84,500,000 or $85,000,000 and that our receipts from taxation have gone up that much. They have gone up $347,200,000, but-
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury:) From all the sources the minister mentioned. I suppose it is not possible to separate the figures and show what was due to the increased rate and what was due to increased business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

That would be a tremendous task, and I could hardly expect the minister to get the figures. But the figures the minister has given are revealing. They are perhaps a little beyond what I had anticipated. Of course the rates are exceedingly high. Has the minister given any consideration to the question whether he has not reached the saturation point in this class of taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should not like to say anything about that at this stage of the session.

There is no harm in flying a kite once in a while. I have been examining a comparatively large number of financial returns as they have been published from time to time in the financial papers, and I have been impressed with this fact, that owing to the very heavy increase in taxation the net profits are, in most instances, away below what they were before the increase in taxation. I am not complaining about that because the country must have the money, but I know of a company which showed a gross profit of $5,400,000, the best in its history. The write-offs for various items reduced that figure to a net of $2,400,000, and because the tax had not been assessed the directors of the company had to appropriate the whole sum and the shareholders got nothing.

I am very glad that the minister answered the leader of the opposition as he did. I think it would be unfortunate if any statement should be made at this time indicating that we have reached the maximum.
I have two interesting tables before me. One is in the account of the budget speech delivered by the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) in 1940, when he was Minister of Finance. On page 17 is a table showing the income tax payable in the different provinces. I notice quite a wide variety of rates. In British Columbia, for example, married persons receiving $500,000-
If any.

-are taxed, according to the 1940 rate, $357,000. There is a provincial tax of $135,000. Elsewhere the provincial rates are approximately:
Alberta	 $145,000
Saskatchewan	 181,000
Manitoba	 50,000
Ontario	   24,000
Quebec and Montreal	 76,000

Is the hon. member sure of that?

How about summer-fallow?

Could the minister
explain how the rate brought down last year was arrived at, as shown on page 15 of his budget speech. speechtext: I shall have to check the statements, to begin with. I think the hon. gentleman has left out any investment surtax, has he not?
I am simply comparing these two similar tables.

speechtext:
I think he has also left

No. The figures I have given are after providing for national defence
tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suggest that, if the hon. member can spare his documents he should send them over. Perhaps I can check them here and give him an answer. I may have to ask him to wait until another day. Usually figures of this sort require a little study before a categorical answer can be given.

It is rather difficult to preserve sequence in this debate. Just before six o'clock the hon. member for Northumberland, New Brunswick, asked certain questions with respect to the gasoline tax and the liquor tax. I was about to ask a question when the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann), who was in the chair, declared that it was six o'clock. We come back at eight o'clock and find that we have to take up an entirely different trend of thought. We were discussing whether there would be any agreement as between the provinces and the dominion government with respect to the lowering of gasoline tax revenues as a result of war conditions. At that time the minister said that there are certain things which we cannot control; that we cannot predicate our taxation on war conditions. I quite appreciate that. But one thing which war conditions do not particularly affect is the revenue derived by the provinces from liquor. I know the minister and all other hon. members realize that, apart from provincial revenues from mining and lumbering-and even those are more or less controlled by the federal government through the controllers whom we have appointed- the greatest provincial revenue comes from liquor taxation. In view of the arrangement made as between the federal government and the provincial governments there is something which I think it is important that the provinces should know, particularly in view of the campaign which is going on from Halifax to Vancouver in favour of curtailing not only the sale but also the manufacture of alcoholic beverages. Would the minister be prepared to say now, so as to give some assurance to the . provinces that are depending on this revenue to carry on their various paternal and social legisative enactments, that the federal government has no idea at the present time of making any change whatsoever in the liquor laws which would adversely affect-
The breweries?

No, the revenue. I am not talking about the breweries alone. I am speaking of revenue. This is the revenue which hon. members connected with the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are always asking about-revenue belonging to the provinces. Is the minister prepared to say that the federal government will not introduce

any legislation which will adversely affect the revenues of the various provinces so far as it is dependent on the sale of alcoholic beverages?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not care to make a commitment of that kind. I wrote the premier of Ontario some months ago that it was not the intention of the dominion government to step into the field of regulation of the sale of liquor, that the dominion considered that that should be left to the provinces; and that is what I do feel about that. I believe that the provinces should assume and properly discharge the responsibility of regulating the sale of liquor. But if the hon. gentleman wants me to go to the length of saying that no legislation will be introduced which may adversely affect the revenue from the sale of liquor, I do not know what the ramifications of that commitment would be, and I would not like to make it.
There is no question about the jurisdiction to do it, though.

The minister perhaps misunderstood me. I realize that his budget may, through taxation, affect indirectly the sale of liquor. What I am getting at is, that the federal government is not prepared to bring down any legislation which will curb sales, apart from the fact that extra taxation may be levied. The federal government does not intend to bring about any question of prohibition in the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The statement I made in my letter to the premier of Ontario, which was given publicity at the time, still stands. It is not our intention to regulate the sale of liquor. That we consider is primarily at least within the jurisdiction of the provinces, and the provinces should assume and discharge that responsibility. I think they are prepared to do so.

The
government is not prepared to exercise any measure of control over the sale of intoxicating liquors, but the question of taxation is quite another matter. The minister distinguishes between the two.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. I can imagine other ways. I do not want to foreshadow anything, because I have nothing in mind as likely to be done, but I can imagine other things that might possibly affect the production of liquor, or something of that kind.
Or the importation.

Yes, something of that kind. I do not know what it may be necessary to

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is unfortunate that the hon. gentleman has not these documents before him so that he can follow what I say. The tax on a married person with no dependents, having an income of $500,000, is now $401,120. That includes national defence tax, but does not include the surcharge on investment income. This was not exactly a new feature, but the tax on investment income was changed last year so that it became a much more important feature of taxation than it was before. This section sets out the additional subsidies during each year of the term of the agreement to the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. On what basis are these five provinces accorded the extra subsidies set out in this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On the second reading of the bill I stated that when section 4 was under discussion I would wish to give the house more information in regard to the principles and considerations which led us to fix upon the fiscal needs subsidies recommended for the three maritime provinces and for Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
Unfortunately, there was no ready-made formula which could be used for this purpose. It was a question of judgment based on a great many factors. Of necessity the decisions had to be somewhat arbitrary, but there were a number of important factors or principles which were taken into account.
In the first place, we considered it preferable to settle once and for all the amounts of the annual payments under the agreement to the provinces, including the fiscal needs subsidies, if any. The alternative would have been for the dominion to review the provincial budgets each year, which would entail a careful and detailed scrutiny of all expenditures.
Would that have been an unmixed evil?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it would have been undesirable.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury); That is, they would resent it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would rather have the hon. gentleman doing it than myself.
Even if the dominion were in a position to do this effectively, which it is not, it would tend to create antagonism and friction between the dominion and the provinces, and in addition would have involved a number of other undesirable factors. Under the circumstances, it seemed wiser to fix the subsidy where one ' was needed at an amount which would permit a province to stand on its own feet until the end of the war without coming back to the dominion for further assistance. This does not, of course, mean that if something in the nature of a national catastrophe should occur, it would not be necessary for us to review the situation again and perhaps take necessary supplemental action.

That is leaving the door open.
Income and Coi~poration Tax

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not very far open. I think the committee will agree that barring such developments of a grave and emergent nature, no province should feel that it has any right to come back to the dominion for further assistance under present conditions.
That is positively closing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As a result of the agreement, it knows pretty well what its total revenues will be; it should know the total amount of cloth available to it and it should cut its coat according to its cloth.
Second, it was desirable to use as far as practicable "objective criteria" as a basis for assessing the financial position of any of the provinces requiring fiscal needs subsidies. This phrase "objective criteria" was used frequently in the discussions with the provinces. In other words, it was desirable that consideration should be given to known facts rather than to hypothetical considerations. This meant that the basic consideration had to be the .financial position of the province during its last completed fiscal year, together with any other known factors which might reasonably be expected to alter such position in the future, but that no attention should be paid to contingencies of an intangible or a speculative nature or provisions for emergency situations.
It will be understood that several of the provinces argued for something of the nature of insurance against emergent situations. They argued that they could not tie themselves up in this way, that they might have to do this and they might have to do that which would cost them money, and that the dominion, if they were fixing these fiscal need subsidies once and for all, would have to take account of possible or certainly probable developments.
In other words, they wanted the dominion to assume responsibility in any emergencies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. I do not say they were unfair about it at all; but the principle we went on was that we could not base our payments upon hypothetical considerations, or possibilities of emergencies, or anything like that.
Third, while some increases in provincial costs may be expected, particularly in connection with cost of living bonuses for civil servants, interest on indebtedness, maintenance of highways and bridges which are being subjected to heavy traffic wherever near army, navy and air force camps, and possibly in certain cases higher salaries to retain public schoolteachers, there should be a reasonable limit to any of such increases in costs in view

of the ceiling which has been placed over prices and wages. Furthermore, these increased costs will be offset partly or wholly by reductions in unemployment relief and by increased revenues.
Fourth, the relative level of costs and services in the different provinces cannot be ignored, but in view of the tremendous sums which the dominion must raise for war expenditures, this was not considered an appropriate time for certain of the provinces to bring their services up to the levels prevailing in other provinces. There is an obligation on all governments to defer until after the war every expenditure which can possibly be avoided.
It was in the light of these general principles and considerations that the fiscal needs subsidies provided for in the bill were determined. In view of their strong budgetary position it was obvious at once that no fiscal needs subsidy could be justified in the case of Ontario, Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia.
In the case of the maritime provinces there was a special situation in view of the fact that the special grants voted annually to these provinces as a result of the recommendations of the Duncan and White commissions represented in fact additional subsidies w'hich the dominion is bound to continue. It was for this reason that a special clause was inserted in the agreements with the maritime provinces to the effect that the dominion recognizes that these grants are in the nature of a subsidy and undertakes to continue paying them upon the termination of the agreement. As the committee is aware, Bill No. 17. has been introduced in order to incorporate this undertaking in dominion legislation so as to avoid any possibility of misunderstanding at a later date.
Under these circumstances none of the maritime provinces could reasonably be expected to enter into the agreement if it was going to result in an out-of-pocket loss to the province on the basis of its 1940 operations. Otherwise the province would be better off if it continued to receive the annual special grant from the dominion and continued to collect the relatively moderate taxes imposed upon its residents. In the case of all three maritime provinces there would have been out-of-pocket losses, and for this reason alone fiscal needs subsidies would have been justified and required.
The subsidy of $325,769.31 which is recommended for Nova Scotia is in fact the amount of the out-of-pocket loss to the province; in other words, the total loss of its fiscal needs subsidy plus the annual payment to be made

Income and Corporation Tax
to Nova Scotia under section 3 of the bill will merely place Nova Scotia in the same position it would have been in if it had retained its special annual grant or subsidy and had not suspended its income and corporation taxes-on the basis of 1940 results from these taxes. Any additional payment was not considered justified in view of the province's strong budgetary position. After making up the out-of-pocket loss referred to, the province would have a surplus of $1,096,000 on the basis of its 1940 operating results after provision for debt retirement. That answers the question as to the basis for the fiscal needs subsidy for Nova Scotia.
In the case of Prince Edward Island, the out-of-pocket loss to the province on the basis of its 1940 operations, had no fiscal needs subsidy been provided for in the agreement, would have been $262,17402, and the province would have had a deficit of $280,000 before making any provision for debt retirement or providing any cushion whatever for possible increases in certain costs. It wTas believed that the dominion should not assume responsibility for placing every province in a position where it could meet its full obligations for sinking funds or debt retirement. To do so would mean that the dominion, out of its own current revenues, would be paying off the capital obligations of a province. Furthermore, the required provisions for sinking funds and debt retirement vary considerably in the different provinces; they are particularly high in Prince Edward Island where they average some 2i per cent of the total debt. On the other hand it could be argued that the dominion should leave the province in a position to make some minimum capital expenditures or, alternatively, to make some moderate provision for sinking funds or debt retirement and, in addition, have something as a cushion against increased costs. In the case of Prince Edward Island, therefore, it is recommended that the dominion should pay a fiscal needs subsidy of $175,000 in addition to the $262,174.02 necessary to make up the loss which, as I have already pointed out, Prince Edward Island would otherwise have suffered under the agreement; this means a total fiscal needs subsidy of $437,174.02. On the basis of the 1940 results this would leave a surplus of $157,000 before provision for sinking funds. A sinking fund provision of one per cent of the province's outstanding debt at December 31, 1940, would be $85,000, leaving $72,000 as a cushion against increased costs. Actually sinking fund requirements were $205,000 in 1940, so that on this basis, after making this very heavy provision for debt retirement and giving effect to all the dominion's proposals, there would have been
a deficit of $48,000 on the basis of 1940 operations. I think that answers the question in regard to Prince Edward Island.
In the case of New Brunswick, the out-ofpocket loss to the province already referred to would have been $71,493.30. It is proposed to make up this loss and to pay, in addition, $300,000 as a fiscal needs subsidy, making a total of $371,493.30. This would leave the province, on the basis of its 1940 operations, with a surplus after provision for normal debt retirement-which is somewhat less than 1 per cent of its total outstanding debt-of $353,000, which we do not consider excessive at all and which we thought was fair. I think that answers the question in regard to New Brunswick.
So much for the maritime provinces. I have still to deal with the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
After deducting the loss of the $750,000 special grant to Manitoba, which was cancelled last year, Manitoba would have had a surplus of $1,040,000 on the basis of its fiscal year ended March 31, 1941, before making any provision for sinking funds or debt retirement. A provision, for this purpose or for capital expenditure, of one per cent of the province s outstanding debt would amount to about $900,000. leaving only $140,000 for increased costs in the future. Costs have been held down and services starved in Manitoba in recent years to a very considerable extent, and some increases are to be expected in the future, particularly for highway maintenance and education. In view of this, it was proposed that Manitoba should be given a fiscal needs subsidy of $600,000 per annum, instead of the special grant of $750,000 which the province had been receiving in recent years.
In the case of Saskatchewan, after giving effect to the new arrangement-apart from any fiscal needs subsidy-the province would have had a deficit of $653,000 on current account for the year ended March 31, 1941, before making any provision for sinking funds or debt retirement. A sinking fund provision of 1 per cent of the outstanding debt would require $1,261,000, which, if added to the deficit of $653,000, would mean a total deficit of $1,914,000. Actually Saskatchewan has not been providing for its full sinking fund requirements for some years, so that it would not be reasonable for the dominion to make up the full amount of the deficiency referred to plus a cushion to take care of any increases in costs. After all the factors were considered, it was decided to recommend that Saskatchewan should be granted a fiscal needs subsidy of $1,500,000 which, after the current

account deficit of $653,000 is deducted, will leave $847,000 for debt retirement or as a cushion for future increases in costs. Actually the provision made by Saskatchewan for debt retirement in its fiscal year ending April 30, 1941, was only $170,000. speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 17, to provide for the payment of additional subsidies to the maritime provinces.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have not prepared any statement with a view to making it on the second reading of this bill. The whole story is found in the preamble to the bill. Briefly I may say that these grants have been voted year by year by parliament, pursuant to the findings of two commissions, the Duncan commission and the White commission.

Maritime Provinces-Subsidies
The maritime provinces considered that since they are forgoing these grants for the period of these agreements, they should have some statutory guarantee that the grants would be resumed at the termination of the agreements. speechtext:
This is very important to us in British Columbia. The hon. member for New Westminster has brought it out in specific terms. I am not grudging the maritimes their subsidy, but they get it automatically under the act. As I understand, however, at the end of this agreement the question comes before parliament whether or not British Columbia continues to receive the $750,000. It is not a question whether the $750,000 is or is not ample; the question whether or not the province gets one dollar must come before this parliament. As a member representing British Columbia I should like a definite statement as to whether the provincial authorities thoroughly understood in agreeing to this new bill, that there was only a possibility of the subsidy of $750,000, which might be classed as a special subsidy, being restored.
There are two things the minister should state, and they are of vital importance to British Columbia. Apparently we do not come under any royal commission or any act of parliament, as do the maritime provinces. I suggest, however, that at least morally it is recognized not only by this government but by the preceding one, that we are entitled to something. It would appear to me that under this bill we from British Columbia would have to appear before the parliament of Canada, at the expiration of the present new bill, asking parliament to grant us a subsidy of $750,000, as a temporary amount pending a final solution. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR PAYMENT OF ADDITIONAL SUBSIDIES
speechtext: As I said before, I do not wish to make any agreement with respect to restoration, because action may depend upon a great many factors. Just consider what the situation is likely to be. These agreements may last three or four or five years. At the end of that time the question will arise as to whether the province will resume the collection of income and corporation taxes, or whether it will not. There will, in all probability, be a completely new arrangement with the provinces. Then, that may not happen; it may be that the agreement will just come to an end, and that there will be no arrangement. The province will simply pick up where it left off. A person cannot foresee what the situation will be. One cannot foresee what concession or new arrangement will be made by the provinces, or between the provinces and the dominion. It may be that at that time this grant will be a very unimportant thing, and that something else will take its place. Possibly something more advantageous will take its place. It may be that the amount will be too small, that it will need to be larger. It may be that no subsidy at all will be required, or that a lesser amount may be required. It is not a settled thing, and I cannot make any commitment or give any undertaking in regard to what the policy of the government in power in Canada at that time will be, or what our policy will be if we are then in office. There are too many factors in the situation which would have some bearing on the matter, and I do not think we should be asked to do anything more than it was agreed at the conference we would do, namely insert a clause protecting such rights as there may be, and put that clause in the agreement, so that it cannot be said at the termination of this agreement that a certain thing went by the board, and that something was forfeited at the time the agreement was entered into. speechtext:

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR PAYMENT OF ADDITIONAL SUBSIDIES

speechtext:

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR PAYMENT OF ADDITIONAL SUBSIDIES
speechtext: I should like to say one word by way of compliment to the Minister of Finance. I am sure British Columbia will be delighted to know that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) is endorsing the action of this government, while the hon. member for Fraser Valley is doing otherwise.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR PAYMENT OF ADDITIONAL SUBSIDIES
speechtext: I do not want the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) to put words in my mouth. I expressed myself quite clearly as to what was done. I am sorry to note that the hon. member for Fraser Valley is out of line, not only with this government but also with the government of British Columbia.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
